rubric.criterion: Identify measured populations as squared amplitudes and the allowed operation as one rotation on two neighboring coordinates, with unreported signs.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for the correct measurement and gate interpretation, explicitly or through a correct computation.

rubric.criterion: Prove necessity of unchanged prefix masses at every cut other than the acted-on edge, using preservation of pair mass and the fixed outside coordinates.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for a correct local invariance or for the prefix observation without its full justification.

rubric.criterion: Prove sufficiency for each compatible signed input. The test enforces agreement outside and equal pair mass, a real rotation reaches a pair with the prescribed populations at positive mass, and the zero-mass case needs no division.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for the outside-and-pair inference, 1 for a justified positive-mass realization valid for all signs, and 1 for the zero-pair case. Equivalent direct arguments earn the same points.

rubric.criterion: List all compatible locations for zero, one, or more than one changed cut, including the permitted identity operation when the reports agree.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for a correct classification of the unequal reports or for correctly identifying all edges in the equal case.

rubric.criterion: Diagnose both numerical reports with the changed cuts or equivalent population calculations.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for each correctly justified diagnosis.

nodes.claim: The reports \(p,q\) are normalized nonnegative vectors, \(p_j=x_j^2\), and output signs are free.
Any real half-angle rotation is available on the selected ordered pair.
The gate fixes the amplitudes outside its pair.
The pair retains squared radius, and each pair on the same positive-radius circle is reachable from any input pair on it. The zero-radius orbit is the origin.
An operation on edge \(i\) leaves every prefix mass except possibly \(P_i\) unchanged.
If all prefix differences except possibly \(D_i\) vanish, finite differencing gives equal outside populations and equal pair totals, including at endpoint cuts.
The inferred local conditions suffice for any fixed signed input: choose a same-radius output pair, apply a rotation sending the actual pair to it, and keep each outside amplitude.
The candidate-edge set consists exactly of the indices \(i\) for which every other cut has zero difference.
When no cut changes, every location is compatible. One changed cut forces its edge, and two or more exclude all locations. The zero-pair and equal-report cases are included.
The cut differences in the two examples are \((0,-1,0)/8\) and \((1,1,1)/8\). The former identifies \((1,2)\), the latter excludes every edge.

joins.why_each: Coordinates away from the edge account for prefixes excluding the pair and the outside portion of larger prefixes. Conservation on the pair accounts for the portion of a prefix containing both sites.

Differencing verifies the necessary numerical compatibility for this pair. The circle orbit realizes the requested inside populations for the actual signs. Fixed outside coordinates preserve the other reported populations.
The invariance argument excludes false locations. Reachability ensures every location that passes the test actually fits.

alternative_routes.assumptions: Valid normalized population reports and arbitrary real angles.
alternative_routes.route: Test pair totals and outside coordinates for each possible edge, construct a rotation by a determinant/dot-product calculation, and convert the entry test into prefix form.

alternative_routes.assumptions: The local pair is nonzero; handle the zero pair separately.
alternative_routes.route: Use transitivity of \(SO(2)\) on the real circle, or a difference of polar arguments, and use neighboring finite differences to invert the cumulative data.

reasoning_map.interpretation: Dependencies below are author-specified local mathematical premises. Source graph edge IDs in the source index express ownership.

common_errors: Treat a population as a signed amplitude, or assume that a single angle must work simultaneously for every unknown sign pattern.
Allow a gate to change any two sites even when they are not adjacent, or infer only from the number of changed individual populations without checking their location.
Demand a changed cut when the two reports agree, or divide by zero for a pair containing no mass.

boundary_cases.conclusion: Every edge is possible with the identity angle. The reports cannot identify a location.
Every rotation fixes that pair. The proposed gate accounts only for an entirely unchanged report.
There is just one edge, and every normalized pair of output populations is attainable for each signed input.

boundary_cases.condition: Two or more prefix masses differ.
boundary_cases.conclusion: No choice of edge or angle explains the reports.

valid_alternatives: Award the full 10 points to any mathematically valid solution answering all requested parts. Methods, intermediate formulas and notation may differ from the reference.
With the given arbitrary real angles, compare \(p,q\) directly outside a candidate pair and compare their local totals. Derive equivalence to the cut test by summing or differencing.

At positive pair mass, subtract the two signed polar arguments, or compose a rotation from the input to the positive radius with a rotation from that radius to the desired pair. At zero pair mass use the identity or any angle.

difficulty.D0_facet: Identify measured populations as squared amplitudes and the allowed operation as one rotation on two neighboring coordinates, with unreported signs.
difficulty.rationale: Derive the prefix test in both directions for every possible input sign, identify all compatible edge locations in the equal-profile and unequal-profile cases, handle a zero pair, and diagnose two exact datasets.

rubric.criterion: Use the specified positive basis input, exact signed target and unit cost per adjacent two-site operation. Identify that only the action on this one input is constrained.
rubric.partial: Award 1 when the cost and equality conventions are correctly expressed or applied.

rubric.criterion: Establish for every circuit that each edge between the extreme sites of the support together with the source must be used. Initially the far side is zero, without the edge it remains zero, and the edges cost separately.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for recognizing the required cuts or proving the obstruction for one cut. Award 2 for applying it to all distinct required cuts and adding their costs.

rubric.criterion: Construct a preparation in at most the hull length: give a legal ordered-edge mechanism for signed pairs in either orientation, apply it throughout the interval while preserving previous work, and obtain the exact signed target from the source within budget.
rubric.partial: Award 1 each for the valid local mechanism, its full traversal including holes, and the input/output sign and gate-count verification. Any equivalent synthesis earns the same points.

rubric.criterion: State the sharp count for positive hull length and both source-only signs. Supply the one-gate sign-flip witness when a neighbor exists and the obstruction for a one-site path.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for the ordinary count and the empty-circuit positive case, and 1 for the negative singleton with its finite or infinite cost and justification.

rubric.criterion: Give the five-gate example count and all minimizing source sites on a general multisite target, with justification.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for each correct part. The example needs the count and a valid justification; an explicit numerical gate list is optional.

nodes.claim: The input is \(+e_s\), the target is a signed real unit vector, and gates are unit-cost adjacent-plane rotations on the path.
If a particular edge is absent, its two components evolve independently. The side initially equal to zero stays identically zero.
Each cut from \(L\) to \(R\) separates \(s\) from at least one nonzero target coordinate. Distinct cuts correspond to distinct legal gates on this path.
Any circuit with a positive-length hull has cost at least \(R-L\), even when it also uses other edges.
On an ordered pair of either orientation one real rotation can fold all signed pair mass into the parent with nonnegative sign. Orthogonality preserves the total norm.
Leaf elimination on the interval rooted at \(s\) uses at most one step per edge, leaves removed coordinates zero, and for \(R>L\) ends at \(+e_s\).
Inverting the elimination produces the exact signed target with at most \(R-L\) steps.
For positive hull length the minimum is \(R-L\).

The sole unit targets on a zero-length hull are \(\pm e_s\); an empty list gives the positive sign. A \(2\pi\) rotation flips the negative sign into reach when \(N\ge2\), while a one-site path has no gate.
The eight-site hull has five edges. For multisite support \([\ell,u]\) is the interval of minimizing source choices, and outside cost increases by the distance to it.

joins.why_each: Omitting the cut edge keeps the side away from the source at zero squared mass. An endpoint of the hull on that side has a nonzero target amplitude of either sign, giving the side strictly positive target squared mass and forcing a gate across this cut.
The interval geometry supplies a leaf order and the number of edges. Signed pair folding supplies the legal local move in that order and the final nonnegative norm.
The bound from graph cuts applies to every competing circuit. The inverse elimination supplies one circuit with the matching cost. Neither result alone identifies the minimum.

alternative_routes.assumptions: One input basis coordinate and an arbitrary signed real target, with arbitrary angles on path edges.
alternative_routes.route: Mark a site as reachable whenever it is connected to the source in the used-edge graph. Its connected component yields the lower bound. A forward traversal distributes subtree norms, selecting final signed values as coordinates are completed.

alternative_routes.assumptions: A positive-length hull; isolated-source signs are handled separately.
alternative_routes.route: Peel left and right toward \(s\) with signed polar angles, or compress either side to a neighbor before the final merge and invert the sequence. Count distinct interval edges and prove all cuts necessary.

reasoning_map.interpretation: Dependencies below are author-specified local mathematical premises. Source graph edge IDs in the source index express ownership.

common_errors: Count nonzero target entries and overlook zero intermediate sites or the transport distance from the source.
Read the length of one chosen sweep or a whole-matrix compiler as a lower bound on every state-preparation circuit.
Ignore the independent signs, including treating the vector \(-e_s\) as identical to \(e_s\), or choose the wrong sign when the parent is the second endpoint.
Return an unreachable sign flip on the one-site path or require a free permutation to place the source.

boundary_cases.conclusion: The optimal empty circuit uses zero gates, including at \(N=1\).
One \(2\pi\) rotation on any incident edge suffices and zero gates cannot suffice.
The minimum is \(+\infty\), since there is no legal gate.

boundary_cases.condition: The support is a single site different from the source.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The minimum is its path distance from \(s\) for either target sign.

boundary_cases.condition: The source lies in a hole between two nonzero target sites.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The hull includes every edge across the hole. For free source choice this interior site is as good as either support extreme.

valid_alternatives: Award the full 10 points to any mathematically valid solution answering all requested parts. The proof may use a different circuit, invariant, example implementation or order of elimination.

For the upper bound, distribute subtree norms forward along the interval rooted at \(s\). At each site keep enough mass for the remaining branches and give each finished coordinate its signed target value. Verify orientations and that every edge is used at most once.

For the lower bound, consider the graph of all used edges, whose connected component at \(s\) contains every nonzero output site. A path component spanning the source and support contains all \(R-L\) edges. This argument also handles circuits visiting extra sites.

difficulty.D0_facet: Use the specified positive basis input, exact signed target and unit cost per adjacent two-site operation. Identify that only the action on this one input is constrained.
difficulty.rationale: Identify all separating cuts forced by the target, show they impose additive gate lower bounds, construct a signed preparation on the intervening path including zero target entries, settle both source-only signs and the one-site obstruction, and optimize source placement on multisite supports.

rubric.criterion: Use the site-matching layer model and squared overlap with the signed real target. One vertex cannot relay through two incident edges in one layer.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for correctly interpreting the layer and score conventions, explicitly or through the derivation.

rubric.criterion: Bound every circuit by a time-ordered set of reached sites and then by their total target weight. Justify support containment with repeated edges or cancellations and use unit norm to control squared fidelity.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for the causal support bound and 1 for the squared-overlap upper bound on the resulting set.

rubric.criterion: Attain the chosen reached-set bound with a legal signed circuit, by first-contact synthesis or any equivalent construction. Treat a zero projection and a singleton reached set with either root sign.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for identifying the optimal signed direction or correctly handling its exceptional cases, and the second for showing that the required direction or score can be synthesized in the given layers.

rubric.criterion: Give the vertex/time recurrence or a mathematically equivalent polynomial recurrence and prove both directions, accounting for distinct child-contact times, residual time and concurrent independent subtrees.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for the correct state, base and optimization rule, 1 for bounding every schedule by it, and 1 for showing its choices form a legal schedule.

rubric.criterion: Justify polynomial time in the stated real arithmetic/comparison model, bounding both the state count and work per state.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for a valid complexity justification, including other polynomial evaluation methods.

rubric.criterion: Compute all three example scores and demonstrate the distance-only failure with a feasible schedule and a necessary depth-two obstruction. Include the zero-budget and singleton-tree values in the general answer.
rubric.partial: Award 1 for these conclusions with sufficient justification by the recurrence or an explicit schedule. Incomplete reasoning on the general upper or lower bound may still earn points above.

nodes.claim: The finite rooted tree, normalized signed target \(a\), weights \(w_v=a_v^2\), source \(+e_r\), and squared overlap score are supplied.
Each layer consists of arbitrary real rotations on disjoint tree edges. A selected pair has a circular orbit, is orthogonal and has an inverse on the same edge.
The monotone marked set for a schedule contains the actual support at every layer: two unmarked endpoints have zero amplitudes. Reuse of edges and cancellations cannot invalidate this upper bound.

First contact on a rooted tree enters from the unique parent in a later layer than the parent was reached. The children of a fixed parent have distinct first-contact layers. Along a branch the times strictly increase.
For each schedule with final marked set \(I\), squared overlap is at most \(m_I=\sum_{v\in I}w_v\), by norm preservation and Cauchy–Schwarz.

If \(m_I>0\), the normalized signed restriction realizes this squared score as a vector in the coordinate subspace. For \(m_I=0\) every supported unit vector has score zero. For \(I=\{r\}\), \(e_r\) has score \(a_r^2\) for either target sign.

On a marked set of size at least two, a signed unit vector compresses to \(+e_r\) along the first contacts taken in reverse layers. Negating and reversing the gates synthesizes that vector within the allotted layers.
The optimum over all circuits equals the maximum total weight of a marked set. This needs the upper bound, an optimal direction and its schedule-respecting realization.

For \(F(v,t)\), every possible schedule yields an assignment of first child contacts to distinct times, with residual time \(t-j\) in the selected subtree. Its marked weight is at most the matching recurrence.

Conversely, distinct child/time assignments and maximizing residual schedules can be combined without endpoint conflicts. Different child subtrees are disjoint, and internal work starts after that child's contact.
The vertex/time table with base \(F(v,0)=w_v\) and maximum-weight child/time matchings gives the optimal marked weight by subtree induction.
Postorder and polynomial-time bipartite matching compute \(F(r,d)\) in polynomially many real operations. Recorded matchings and signed rotations give a circuit attaining that squared fidelity.

The score is \(a_r^2\) at zero budget and one for a one-vertex tree. The specified tree gives \(0,1/2,1\) at depths one through three. Parent contention at the first layer precludes both distance-two targets by layer two.

joins.why_each: Target weights specify the relevant coordinate projection, gate orthogonality supplies output norm one, and support containment permits restriction of the inner product to the marked coordinates.

The local orbit and inverse give a legal signed fold and its undo. The temporal parent relation ensures descendants are empty before their parent is folded and that the original layer budget is respected.

The projection bound limits arbitrary circuits. The optimal direction identifies the score and handles zero mass and singleton cases. Signed synthesis ensures an optimal direction on any nontrivial positive-mass marked set can be realized under its schedule.
The assignment extracted from every schedule supplies the upper inequality. Independently executable child schedules realize the candidate sums and supply the reverse inequality.
The table optimizes total marked weight. Its equality with attainable signed fidelity is needed for the same table to solve the requested state objective.

alternative_routes.assumptions: Finite rooted tree, arbitrary real edge rotations, matching layers, and the stated squared fidelity.
alternative_routes.route: Use a forward broadcast schedule. Assign child subtrees to time slots through polynomial matching or flow, realize the normalized projection by successive subtree-norm splits, and bound arbitrary outputs by causal support.

alternative_routes.assumptions: Induction on subtree height with the same endpoint-disjoint model and real arithmetic.
alternative_routes.route: Use an equivalent time-expanded assignment formulation for the recurrence. Prove both inequalities by restricting schedules and joining subtrees. Signed edge rotations or inverse elimination certify realizability.

reasoning_map.interpretation: Dependencies below are author-specified local mathematical premises. Source graph edge IDs in the source index express ownership.

common_errors: Replace feasible reached sets by graph balls or by arbitrary subsets of those balls, permitting two children to receive their first contacts simultaneously from one parent.
Use \(t-j+1\) residual layers, or let a child relay during its birth layer.

Treat a projection bound as attained without constructing its signed direction or an equally good output; normalize a zero projection or insist on a negative root representative when the singleton output already attains the score.
Restrict competitors to a particular sweep or to circuits that never revisit an edge without proving the universal upper bound.
Enumerate every child ordering as the algorithm without a polynomial way to optimize, or award a whole subtree when the remaining layers cannot reach it.

boundary_cases.conclusion: Only \(e_r\) is produced, so the score is \(a_r^2\).
No edge is available. Since \(a_r=\pm1\), the score of \(e_r\) equals one.
Every output supported on the reached vertices gives score zero. There is no normalized projected direction.
The negative normalized projection need not be attainable. The actual \(+e_r\) has the same squared score.

boundary_cases.condition: An ancestor has zero target mass and a descendant has positive target mass.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The ancestor may temporarily carry amplitude and transmit it before its required final zero. Its inclusion in a schedule can be necessary to reach a valuable descendant.

boundary_cases.condition: Both example grandchildren are within distance two.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Depth two reaches at most one of them, whereas three layers reach both.

valid_alternatives: Award the full 10 points to any mathematically valid solution answering all requested parts. A different recurrence, scheduling proof or signed construction earns full credit when it satisfies the problem.

With unrestricted real rotations, distribute subtree norms forward along increasing first-contact times, choosing each finished amplitude with the required sign. Treat zero retained mass and a singleton set at the score level.

Use polynomial min-cost flow, a dummy-augmented assignment algorithm or an equivalent layered-tree dynamic program if it accounts for parent contact capacity, residual time and attainable signed fidelity.
Potential reachability that ignores cancellations, or actual first nonzero transmissions, can establish the universal upper bound provided it is justified for arbitrary circuits.

difficulty.D0_facet: Use the site-matching layer model and squared overlap with the signed real target. One vertex cannot relay through two incident edges in one layer.
difficulty.rationale: Bound arbitrary circuits by the coordinates reachable along time-ordered contacts, construct signed states on the chosen coordinates, join this with the sharp projection bound, solve the child scheduling problem by a polynomial dynamic program, and certify all requested depths on a tree where radius alone overstates fidelity.

rubric.criterion: D0 basis-action facet. Gives both the intermediate-label phase \(a(x)b(p(x))\) and the output \(q(p(x))\) of the chronological product, with the column action or an equivalent explanation.
rubric.partial: One point for the correct composed output or the correctly transported phase with the other part missing or incorrect.

rubric.criterion: Gives \(g=f\circ p\), justifies uniqueness by basis coefficients or conjugation, and establishes the exact equality criterion \(f\circ p=f\) in both directions.
rubric.partial: One point for the correct table without its uniqueness or exactness test, or a correct exactness test without the full table argument.

rubric.criterion: Proves that a single input-independent unit scalar must relate the two column coefficients and that this condition suffices. Either orientation of the scalar is accepted when used consistently.
rubric.partial: One point for the correct common-ratio condition with incomplete justification, or for deriving pointwise ratios while missing the need for the same scalar across cycles.

rubric.criterion: Obtains the transported controlled-NOT table and determines all angles for both uncorrected tests. Explains why a fixed column forces the scalar and why a moved column fixes the angle; an equivalent whole-matrix argument earns full credit.
rubric.partial: One point for the corrected table or a correct conclusion about the angles with insufficient reasoning about the fixed and moved labels.

rubric.criterion: Supplies any normalized two-term input giving orthogonal outputs at the stated angle, verifies the orthogonality, and explains the agreement of computational-basis probabilities for each basis input.
rubric.partial: One point for a valid orthogonality example with incomplete verification or without the probability comparison, or for a valid explanation of basis-input indistinguishability without an orthogonal witness.

nodes.claim: An input basis column \(x\) of \(M(a,p)\) has coefficient \(a(x)\) at its routed row \(p(x)\). In the question all weights have modulus one.
Applying a second factor multiplies the coefficient by \(b(p(x))\) and maps the output label to \(q(p(x))\).
Comparing the two orders on each basis column fixes \(g(x)=f(p(x))\) uniquely.
Leaving the original table gives exact equality if and only if it is constant along each orbit.
Leaving the original table gives global-phase equality precisely when the unit ratios \(f(p(x))/f(x)\) are constant over the whole input set.
On the two labeled bits the controlled NOT sends \((c,t)\) to \((c,t\oplus c)\) with weight one, and the single-target phase table has weight \(e^{i\theta t}\).
The transported table is \(e^{i\theta(t\oplus c)}\), giving ratio one for \(c=0\) and ratios \(e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}\) for \(c=1\).
Both uncorrected tests pass exactly at \(\theta\in2\pi\mathbb Z\). Unchanged labels force the global scalar to be one, and a moved label then forces \(e^{i\theta}=1\).

At \(\theta=\pi\) the orders differ by opposite signs on the two control sectors. An equal-weight superposition from the two sectors gives orthogonal outputs. The basis probabilities still depend only on the routed label.

joins.why_each: The general rewrite identifies which argument to supply, and the control-target gate data give the concrete argument and the three ratios.
The exact and scalar tests are distinct requested conclusions. The computed ratios fix the scalar and supply the necessary and sufficient angle condition for both.
The signed ratios distinguish two coherent components. Single-column support and modulus one explain why the basis-input distributions still coincide.

alternative_routes.assumptions: Any finite nonempty label set, a permutation, and the stated unit-modulus diagonal.
alternative_routes.route: Conjugate the diagonal by the permutation, or multiply the matrices entrywise. Equality and scalar equality then reduce to comparing diagonal entries.

alternative_routes.assumptions: The use of \(\theta=\pi\) and the stated two-bit orientation.
alternative_routes.route: Form the relative operator between the two uncorrected orders. It has eigenvalues of opposite sign on the two control sectors, so a normalized balanced two-sector input has zero output overlap.

reasoning_map.interpretation: Dependencies below are author-specified local mathematical premises. Source graph edge IDs in the source index express ownership.

common_errors: Evaluating both factors at \(x\), or reversing \(q\circ p\), drops the intermediate label on which the second factor acts.
Using \(f\circ p^{-1}\) in the stated input-side rewrite can go undetected in the involutive controlled-NOT example. It fails for a general permutation.
Allowing one scalar per cycle certifies a blockwise relation. The prompt asks for one scalar on the full operator.
Using only the moved columns at \(\theta=\pi\) misses the unchanged columns. An example supported only on the moved labels acquires one common minus sign and cannot demonstrate orthogonality.
Coincidence of probabilities for each basis input determines the routed label, but discards the phase needed for the superposition check.

boundary_cases.condition: The phase table is constant on each cycle, with values allowed to differ between cycles.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The exact rewrite passes because \(f(p(x))=f(x)\) everywhere.

boundary_cases.condition: The permutation has a fixed point and a common-ratio solution exists.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The nonzero weight at that point forces \(\lambda=1\), so the uncorrected rewrite is exact.

boundary_cases.condition: The two-bit gates are tested only on single computational-basis inputs.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Both gate orders have the same one-point output distribution at every angle, even when the coherent operators disagree.

valid_alternatives: For the stated finite basis, entrywise multiplication with its single surviving summand, direct ket action, or \(P_p^\dagger D_fP_p=D_{f\circ p}\) gives the complete transport argument. No full matrix or decomposition into gates is required.

With the same finite nonempty \(X\) and unit-modulus weights, a cyclewise description \(f(p^j x)=\lambda^j f(x)\) is equivalent if the same \(\lambda\) works on every cycle. In this description \(\lambda^{|C|}=1\) automatically on each cycle. The constant-ratio test already expresses both necessity and sufficiency.

Under the stated control-first convention, any equal-probability pair drawn from the control-zero and control-one sectors at \(\theta=\pi\) provides a witness, with an arbitrary relative input phase. Computing the overlap by a relative diagonal matrix or directly showing opposite relative signs earns the same credit.

difficulty.D0_facet: D0 basis-action facet. Gives both the intermediate-label phase \(a(x)b(p(x))\) and the output \(q(p(x))\) of the chronological product, with the column action or an equivalent explanation.
difficulty.rationale: Act on one basis ket to obtain weight \(a(x)b(p(x))\) and label \(q(p(x))\). Identify \(g=f\circ p\) and prove uniqueness. Give both directions of the exact orbit-invariance test and the single-constant test for \(f(p(x))/f(x)\), with a fixed sign convention for that constant. On two bits compute the table \(e^{i\theta(t\oplus c)}\), use the fixed control-zero columns to fix any common phase, and use a moved column to identify all angles. At \(\theta=\pi\) propagate a normalized two-term input through both orders, establish orthogonality, and explain equality of the basis-input output probabilities.

rubric.criterion: D0 basis-action facet. Derives an edge-by-edge condition equivalent to the exact operator equation, with the input conjugation and orientation correct. For example \(d_{p(x)}=(b_x/a_x)d_x\).
rubric.partial: One point for the correct propagated coefficient or edge test with an incomplete derivation, or for a valid starting computation with a later ratio error.

rubric.criterion: Proves that the labeled product on each cycle is necessary and, without fixed references, is a complete invariant. The latter direction may follow from the general construction elsewhere in the answer.
rubric.partial: One point for the necessary product with no sufficiency argument, or for a valid unpinned construction without explicitly identifying the complete invariant.

rubric.criterion: Gives and justifies the extra criterion imposed by multiple references on a cycle, via forward arc products, a base-reference computation, a base-independent residual, or another equivalent test.
rubric.partial: One point for correctly transporting to another reference without stating how to check all pins, or for a correct full test whose necessity or sufficiency remains unexplained.

rubric.criterion: Constructs all diagonal solutions, shows cycle closure and unit modulus, and accounts for the exact freedom for zero, one or several pins on a cycle and for the fixed-point case. A general construction that plainly covers these cases suffices.
rubric.partial: One point for a valid particular calibration with incomplete treatment of freedom or boundary cases, or for the correct freedom without a verified construction.

rubric.criterion: Provides unit weights for two devices on the same permutation with equal products on every labeled cycle and gives two distinct reference labels on a common cycle whose specified values contradict transport along an identified arc.
rubric.partial: One point for a valid example with incomplete verification of its cycle products or incompatible arc, or for explaining the reference conflict without furnishing all data for an example.

nodes.claim: Each device has one nonzero coefficient at \(p(x)\) in column \(x\), namely its unit edge weight.
The calibration is diagonal unitary and some vertex phases are prescribed. Its adjoint acts on \(|x\rangle\) by \(\overline{d_x}\).
The matrix identity holds exactly when \(d_{p(x)}=r_xd_x\) on every edge, with \(r_x=b_x/a_x\in\mathbb T\).
Iterating gives \(d_{p^j(v)}=R(v,j)d_v\), where \(R\) is the product of ratios in the forward direction and the empty product is one.
Each complete loop needs unit ratio product, equivalently equality of the two edge products on that labeled cycle.
Pins on the same cycle must obey \(\eta_t=R(s,j)\eta_s\) along the forward arc from \(s\) to \(t\).

Propagating from one starting vertex builds a unit diagonal. Closure checks the last edge and, when pins exist, arc tests certify every prescribed value. The construction therefore proves sufficiency.
Every solution is determined by its starting phases, which are free once per unpinned cycle and fixed on a pinned cycle. This gives product completeness without pins and the fixed-point description.
On one transposition the assignments \((1,1)\) and \((-1,-1)\) have equal total products, yet pins \((1,1)\) violate the first forward-edge ratio.

joins.why_each: The common routing identifies the matrix entry to compare; diagonal action and its adjoint supply the output and input factors in that coefficient.
Path transport produces the vertex phases, full-loop consistency closes the omitted edge, and reference consistency enforces external values. The last check is vacuous on a cycle with no pins.
The counterexample must pass the product test while failing the pin test, so both facts must be checked on the same labeled cycle.

alternative_routes.assumptions: Each edge ratio lies on the unit circle and the graph of a finite permutation consists of cycles.
alternative_routes.route: A spanning forest with one omitted closing edge per cycle implements the recurrence. Check the omitted chords and propagate any prescribed roots to handle multiple pins.

alternative_routes.assumptions: All phase equations are interpreted modulo \(2\pi\).
alternative_routes.route: Solve additive difference equations along each cycle. A zero sum around each cycle and consistent pinned angle differences are equivalent to the multiplicative conditions.

reasoning_map.interpretation: Dependencies below are author-specified local mathematical premises. Source graph edge IDs in the source index express ownership.

common_errors: Reversing \(b_x/a_x\) while keeping the direction \(x\mapsto p(x)\) solves the oppositely oriented calibration unless all ratios happen to equal their inverses.
A product over every label of \(X\) can agree while individual cycles fail closure. Distinct labeled cycles require separate conditions.
Matching cycle totals alone discards an obstruction between two reference labels on the same cycle.
Testing arcs from a base without checking the closing edge can yield apparent agreement at every reference with an inconsistent full loop.
A single common phase across all cycles undercounts the solutions. Allowing a new freely chosen phase after a pinned base overcounts them.

boundary_cases.condition: A cycle has no references.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Only its closed product must match; each initial unit phase gives one solution on that cycle.

boundary_cases.condition: A cycle has exactly one reference.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Closure is still required, but a consistent cycle has a unique calibration on that component.

boundary_cases.condition: A pinned cycle has multiple references.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Any incompatible reference-to-reference ratio rules out a solution, including when its closed product is correct.

boundary_cases.condition: A fixed point \(p(x)=x\).
boundary_cases.conclusion: The edge coefficient is unchanged by calibration. The weights must agree, and its phase is free or fixed according to the pin.

valid_alternatives: For arbitrary finite nonempty \(X\) with the given unit edge weights, delete one edge of each cycle, propagate weights along the remaining directed path, and check the deleted edge and all pins. Any base choice, including an unpinned base on a pinned cycle, is valid when the base value is fixed by the transported reference.

With the same hypotheses, unpinned equivalence can first be established by reducing both edge tables to a representative with all weights one except the closing edge. Track the resulting vertex phases and their allowed constant factors on each component to impose the reference constraints and recover all solutions.

Choosing angles in \(\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)\) converts edge multiplication into differences. The cycle sum must vanish modulo \(2\pi\) and arc sums must equal the differences of pinned angles. Any consistent choices of representatives receive full credit.

Any finite example with the same labeled permutation, unit weights, matching products on each cycle, and a violated prescribed reference ratio on a single cycle satisfies the diagnostic. The example may use nonreal phases or more than two vertices.

difficulty.D0_facet: D0 basis-action facet. Derives an edge-by-edge condition equivalent to the exact operator equation, with the input conjugation and orientation correct. For example \(d_{p(x)}=(b_x/a_x)d_x\).
difficulty.rationale: Derive the edge equation \(d_{p(x)}=(b_x/a_x)d_x\). Prove full-cycle consistency and compatibility of reference ratios with products of \(b_x/a_x\) along forward arcs. Show the cycle products classify an unpinned labeled cycle under diagonal conjugation, construct the phases from a base choice for each cycle, and show that every solution is obtained. An unpinned cycle has one free unit scalar, and a compatible pinned cycle has none. Include one reference, several references and fixed points. Construct two candidate devices with equal cycle products but inconsistent prescribed endpoints on a single cycle, and identify the specific failing arc.

rubric.criterion: D0 basis-action facet and its trace consequence. Tracks the label and phase after iteration of one edge, identifies return precisely at multiples of the cycle length, and derives the global power trace including the multiplicity factor \(|C|\). An equivalent cycle-block derivation of the same facts is accepted.
rubric.partial: One point for a correctly transported iterate or return condition with an incomplete trace count, or for a correct trace formula with insufficient justification of the cycle contribution.

rubric.criterion: Derives the factor \(z^{|C|}-h_C\) on a cycle and obtains the global characteristic polynomial by the invariant direct sum, with the stated characteristic-polynomial sign convention.
rubric.partial: One point for the correct factorization without a sufficient per-cycle argument, or for a correct per-cycle calculation with the global combination missing.

rubric.criterion: Proves exact recovery on every labeled cycle when lengths are distinct, using only the promised traces and permutation. Accounts for all shorter divisor contributions, or gives a correct alternative which establishes uniqueness and provides a way to compute the values.
rubric.partial: One point for recovery at the smallest or mutually nondividing lengths, or for recognizing a recursive subtraction without determining the divisor contributions correctly.

rubric.criterion: Exhibits two realizable unit-modulus edge assignments for the same permutation with two fixed points and two transpositions, proves equality of all positive power traces, and shows that at least one within-length multiset differs. A construction through realizable cycle products is sufficient.
rubric.partial: One point for a valid collision with incomplete verification, or for explaining an actual factor ambiguity without completing the assignments on the specified permutation. Only swapping labels inside one length does not show multiset ambiguity.

rubric.criterion: Obtains the length-sector power sums with the correct scale, recovers the multiset with multiplicity from the supplied number of reports, and proves the precise uniqueness condition for assigning products to cycle labels. Reassignment invariance and realizability may be shown by exchanging tables between equal-length cycles.
rubric.partial: One point for correct multiset recovery without the full labeled uniqueness boundary, or a correct argument about permutation ambiguity without deriving recovery with multiplicities.

nodes.claim: The known permutation decomposes the labels into disjoint cycles, and the column at \(x\) of \(U\) is the unit edge weight times \(|p(x)\rangle\).
An \(n\)-step walk ends at \(p^n(x)\) with the product of its \(n\) encountered edge weights. One complete cycle multiplies any of its basis vectors by its cycle product.
The length-\(\ell\) cycle restriction has characteristic polynomial \(z^\ell-h_C\) by a cyclic basis, and the invariant direct sum multiplies those factors.
Counting all returning input labels gives \(t_n=\sum_{C:\,|C|\mid n}|C|h_C^{n/|C|}\).
When the known lengths are distinct, increasing-length recovery from \(t_\ell\) subtracts the known contributions of every shorter divisor and isolates one labeled product.
On the specified six-label permutation there are unit tables with length-one products \(\{1,-1\}\) versus \(\{i,-i\}\) and length-two products \(\{-1,1\}\) versus \(\{1,1\}\).

Applying the spectral factor formula to those tables gives the identical polynomial \((z^2-1)^2(z^2+1)\). The unitaries therefore have equal power traces for all positive powers and different within-length product multisets.
The additional measurements project onto all cycles of a specified length and use exponents \(k\ell\) for \(1\leq k\leq m_\ell\). Newton’s identities for complex roots are available.
For every occurring length, the supplied projected traces divide by \(\ell\) to give the first \(m_\ell\) power sums of the products on that length.
The first \(m_\ell\) complex power sums uniquely determine the monic polynomial of degree \(m_\ell\), hence the multiset of cycle products including all repeated roots.
Each reassignment of given products to cycles of the same length can be realized by placing one prescribed unit weight per cycle. The global and projected traces remain unchanged.
The recovered data determine all labels at a given length exactly when its multiset is constant. Unequal products can be exchanged to give different labeled assignments.

joins.why_each: The known distinct lengths identify the target cycle and the smaller indices to consider. The trace equation gives the actual coefficients and powers to subtract.
The example supplies realizable, genuinely different within-length multisets. The characteristic factorization verifies equality of the observational data for every power.
Orbit iteration gives the returning phase on each selected label. The projection and exponents specify precisely which labels and how many powers are observable.
Polynomial reconstruction gives all values with multiplicity. Physical realizability and measurement invariance justify ambiguity when unequal values can exchange labels.

alternative_routes.assumptions: The index set is finite and all edge phases are nonzero unit complex numbers.
alternative_routes.route: Use a cyclic block eigenvector recurrence and sum roots of unity to derive both the spectral factor and the positive trace formula.

alternative_routes.assumptions: Lengths are pairwise distinct and all of \(t_1,\ldots,t_N\) are available exactly.
alternative_routes.route: Recover the global reciprocal polynomial by Newton’s identities, and then successively extract the coefficient at the least remaining cycle length after dividing out shorter factors.

alternative_routes.assumptions: The two tables are on the same specified cycle pattern and every edge has unit modulus.
alternative_routes.route: Verify a collision directly from the trace sum, or through common eigenvalues; show separately that the product multiset changes within at least one length.

reasoning_map.interpretation: Dependencies below are author-specified local mathematical premises. Source graph edge IDs in the source index express ownership.

common_errors: Summing over all cycles at power \(n\) forgets to restrict to \(|C|\mid n\); omitting \(|C|\) counts only one returning label per cycle.

From \(U^\ell=h_C I\) alone one knows that the minimal polynomial divides \(z^\ell-h_C\). A cyclic vector, eigenvector recurrence, determinant, or equivalent argument is needed to get the full degree-\(\ell\) characteristic factor.
Taking \(h_\ell=t_\ell/\ell\) for every distinct length ignores interference from any shorter occurring divisors.
Swapping two different products between equal-length cycles leaves their multiset unchanged. It only proves ambiguity of labeling, which is weaker than the global-trace obstruction requested.
Factoring the global characteristic polynomial into linear factors recovers the eigenvalues, but does not always determine which roots came from \(z^\ell-h_C\) factors of each length.
Length-resolved data are symmetric under permutation of equal-length cycles. Repeated roots still have well-defined multiplicities, and their equality can make labels uniquely determined.

boundary_cases.condition: A cycle has length one.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Its edge phase is its product and its characteristic factor is linear. It contributes at every positive power.

boundary_cases.condition: The smallest occurring length is \(\ell>1\), or an occurring length has no smaller occurring divisor.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The recursion starts at \(h_\ell=t_\ell/\ell\) when this length occurs exactly once and there are no shorter divisor contributions.

boundary_cases.condition: The monic polynomial reconstructed from the first \(m_\ell\) projected power sums has a repeated root.
boundary_cases.conclusion: Newton reconstruction retains multiplicities. If every root is the same value, all cycles of that length have that unique labeled value.

boundary_cases.condition: Two different products occur at the same length.
boundary_cases.conclusion: The whole multiset is known after the length-sector measurements, but exchanging the two products gives two different labeled assignments with the same data.

valid_alternatives: On the given finite-dimensional unitary blocks over \(\mathbb C\), compute the characteristic factor by a determinant expansion, the companion form, a cyclic-vector/minimal-polynomial argument, or an eigenvector recurrence for all roots of \(z^\ell=h_C\). Summing the powers of these roots also proves the trace formula without direct diagonal-entry counting.

For exact complex data and pairwise distinct cycle lengths, Newton’s identities on \(t_1,\ldots,t_N\) give the global characteristic polynomial. After shorter-length factors have been recovered and divided off, work with the residual reciprocal polynomial \(\prod_{d\text{ remaining}}(1-h_d y^d)\). Its coefficient of the smallest remaining degree \(\ell\) is \(-h_\ell\). Repeating supplies an alternative to the divisor recursion.

For the six-label case, any realizable factor swap giving different within-length product multisets is valid. For example use opposite fixed-point phases \(u,-u\) in one assignment and \(v,-v\) in the other, exchange the matching transposition products \(v^2\) and \(u^2\), and retain the same other transposition. For unit \(u,v\) with \(u^2\ne v^2\), the two characteristic polynomials agree. A direct all-power trace calculation is equally sufficient.

For each length sector, any exact reconstruction of the monic polynomial from its first \(m_\ell\) power sums earns credit, including Newton’s identities or a truncated determinant-generating series. An argument via a bijection of equal-length cycles instead of a one-edge realization also establishes the possible assignments to labels.

difficulty.D0_facet: D0 basis-action facet and its trace consequence. Tracks the label and phase after iteration of one edge, identifies return precisely at multiples of the cycle length, and derives the global power trace including the multiplicity factor \(|C|\). An equivalent cycle-block derivation of the same facts is accepted.
difficulty.rationale: Iterate the basis action and separate fixed labels of a power from nonreturning labels. Show that a length-\(\ell\) orbit contributes \(z^\ell-h_C\) to \(\det(zI-U)\) and contributes \(\ell h_C^{n/\ell}\) to \(t_n\) only when \(\ell\mid n\). For distinct lengths recover the product on the unique length-\(\ell\) cycle from \(t_\ell\) after subtracting all shorter divisor contributions, including the base case. With two fixed points and two transpositions, realize two assignments by unit phases and verify a common characteristic polynomial or equality of every trace, together with different within-length multisets. For the augmented observations, divide length-resolved traces by \(\ell\), use the first \(m_\ell\) power sums to reconstruct the monic polynomial of cycle products and all root multiplicities. Show that within-length permutations of products leave the reports invariant, and characterize unique labeled assignment for each length, including the cases of one cycle or identical products.
